worksheet.title: Put It in Order
worksheet.subtitle: Four steps in the right order
worksheet.learning_goal: I can put four steps in order from first to last.

parts.title: Bit's plant grows step by step
parts.text: Bit's plant grows a new leaf each day: 1 leaf, then 2, then 3, then 4. The steps go in order from fewest to most.

parts.title: Write the order
parts.prompt: Write 1, 2, 3, 4 under the mixed-up steps to put them in order (fewest leaves to most).

parts.title: Which is first? Which is last?
parts.prompt: Circle the step that is FIRST (1 leaf). Put an X on the step that is LAST (4 leaves).

parts.title: You try — draw the next step
parts.prompt: After 4 leaves comes day 5. Draw the next step (5 leaves).

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: Putting several steps in the right order makes a plan. A plan of ordered steps is an algorithm — and computers follow them step by step.

teacher_guide.title: Put It in Order
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key
teacher_guide.footer_topic: 3. Put It in Order — Teacher Guide

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Children put four steps in order from fewest leaves to most, and add the next step. Arranging several steps in order is the heart of a plan a computer can follow one step at a time. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start (no computer needed)
parts.text: No computer — paper and a pencil or crayon. You read each prompt aloud; the child answers by circling or numbering. Optional: real objects or cards to put in order by hand first.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 15 minutes)
text: 1. Show them (you do). Line up cards with 1, 2, 3, 4 leaves in order — each day grows one more leaf.
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — number the mixed-up cards in order from fewest to most.
3. Let them try. Children mark first and last (Ex 2), then draw the next step — 5 leaves (Ex 3).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — the four cards show 4, 2, 1, and 3 leaves. Under each card, write its order from fewest to most: the 1-leaf card is 1, the 4-leaf card is 4.
Exercise 2 — circle the 1-leaf card (first); put an X on the 4-leaf card (last). Exercise 3 — draw a step with 5 leaves.

parts.title: If children get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: numbering left-to-right by position. Count the leaves on each card first.
Make it easier: order just three cards before doing four.
Make it harder: ask what day 6 would look like (6 leaves).
Make it active: have four children hold leaf cards and order themselves fewest to most.

parts.title: Ontario Kindergarten link (official wording)
text: Problem Solving and Innovating — children order a multi-step process.
In plain terms: arranging several steps into the right order — the start of a plan (an algorithm).
No reading is needed from the child — you read each prompt aloud; the child answers by circling, numbering, or drawing arrows.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child orders the four steps fewest to most and draws a correct fifth step.
